edge.title: The screenshot that isn't money
edge.setup: You're selling a phone, or you run a small counter. The buyer holds up a UPI success screen — right amount, right name, a reference number, 'bank server is slow, it'll reflect in an hour'. They're already walking away with the goods. There are apps whose only purpose is generating that screen.
edge.tell: Confirmation came from their screen, not from your bank.
move: Only your own SMS, bank app balance, or payment-device voice alert counts. Nothing on their phone is evidence.
Say the sentence plainly: 'I'll hand it over when my bank confirms.' It is not rude; it's the norm.
For sales, meet inside a bank branch or a busy shop — not a parking lot.
edge.why: Trust normally travels with money. Screenshots break that link by making the proof forgeable and instant. Every defence restores the link: confirmation must arrive through a channel the other person cannot author.
edge.variants: Same shape: forged NEFT receipts, fake courier-dispatch proofs, 'payment initiated' emails from a lookalike domain.

lens.name: Induced demand
lens.one_line: Adding road capacity creates new trips that fill it, so congestion returns at a higher throughput.
lens.detail: People who had given up on a route — shifted their timing, taken transit, moved closer — return once it gets easier. The new lane doesn't serve the old traffic; it reveals suppressed demand that was always there. Measured honestly, travel time often lands back where it started within a few years, now with more vehicles.
elsewhere: Build more parking and more people drive in.
Add engineers to a late project and the scope expands to absorb them.
Widen a hospital's OPD and the waiting room refills.
lens.test: When someone promises more capacity will fix congestion, ask: what was suppressed, and what happens when it comes back?
lens.today: Bengaluru is planning 120 km of elevated corridors at ₹23,165 crore, with toll on stretches over 10 km (Moneycontrol), and the Deputy CM spoke of 500 km of new roads (The Times of India). Induced demand says the people who gave up on these routes will return once they get easier, so judge a new road by what it adds to the whole trip and not by its first month.

moved.what: The Supreme Court has cleared Blue Line work at Hebbal, but a construction material shortage after a Tamil Nadu ban is hitting the project (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: Expect work to restart around Hebbal while supply is tight, so do not plan around a Blue Line opening date and keep an alternative for the Hebbal–Tin Factory run.

moved.what: Bengaluru's electorate has fallen from 1.03 crore to 59 lakh after the SIR, a 43% cut, and the city accounts for 40% of deletions statewide (The Hindu, The Times of India).
moved.so_what: Search your name in the final roll today. If you moved flats recently you are more likely to be missing, and fixing it is easier now than near an election.

moved.what: Bengaluru is to get 120 km of elevated corridors at ₹23,165 crore, with toll on stretches longer than 10 km (Moneycontrol).
moved.so_what: A faster elevated route may come with a toll, so when it opens price the toll against the minutes saved, and do not make a house-or-job move on a corridor that has no opening date.

moved.what: Hennur–Bagalur road work, delayed by 18 months, now has a December deadline (The Indian Express).
moved.so_what: Treat December as a target and not a promise: if that road is on your route, keep your current detour through the winter.

moved.what: A woman caught a man recording her inside a Bengaluru metro; he fled with her phone (The Hindu).
moved.so_what: In a crowded coach keep your phone away from the door side and out of one-hand reach, and if someone films you, tell metro staff and the police on the spot, before he gets off.

carry_over.prompt: You are about to pay the printed MRP on a medicine you buy every month: what is the one thing to remember about that number?
carry_over.answer: MRP is the most a seller may charge, not what the product cost and not a price you have to pay.
